extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) staff, administrative law judges, and attorneys involved in USPTO disciplinary matters
extracted.subtask_short: USPTO disciplinary proceeding for patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings under 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. part 11: defining misconduct (conflicts, competence, communications), burden/standard of proof, and factors for sanctions. Includes procedural rules for hearings and practitioner duties during suspension/reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority to regulate and discipline practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for practice before it and to suspend or exclude practitioners; authority flows from 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) and 35 U.S.C. § 32; disciplinary proceedings are conducted under 37 C.F.R. part 11 and section 7 of the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 556, by an impartial hearing officer appointed by USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the jurisdictional and procedural framework for evaluating practitioner conduct. Disciplinary hearings must provide notice and an opportunity for hearing. Citation examples: Kroll v. Finnerty; Sperry v. Florida.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard and burden of proof: clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director bears the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence; the respondent bears the burden of proving affirmative defenses by clear and convincing evidence. 'Clear and convincing' requires evidence producing a firm belief or conviction that facts are highly probable (intermediate between 'beyond a reasonable doubt' and 'preponderance of the evidence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authorities/citations (e.g., Jimenez v. DaimlerChrysler; Colorado v. New Mexico) to define the weight required. Evaluators should assess whether evidence produces an 'abiding conviction' that allegations are 'highly probable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must provide competent representation, which requires the legal, scientific, and technical knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation. A practitioner must know applicable rules or inform themselves of them when representing clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes recognizing ethical duties (e.g., conflict rules) relevant to the matter. Failure to recognize obvious conflicts or ignorance of the disciplinary rules may constitute incompetence. Example from case: respondent's failure to recognize conflicts and unfamiliarity with post-2013 rules supported a §11.101 violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent conflicts of interest prohibition (37 C.F.R. § 11.107)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may not represent a client if the representation involves a concurrent conflict of interest — a significant risk that representation will be materially limited by the practitioner's personal interests. The rule allows an exception only if the client gives informed consent and (where required) that consent is confirmed in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a practitioner's personal or business interests create a 'significant risk' of materially limiting representation. Check that any such conflict was disclosed and that informed consent (where the rule requires) was obtained and confirmed in writing. Example: joint inventorship plus ownership interest created a concurrent conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business transactions with clients (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner is prohibited from entering into a business transaction with a client, or acquiring an ownership, possessory, security or other pecuniary interest adverse to a client, unless the transaction meets specific requirements — including that the client is advised in writing to seek independent legal counsel and gives informed consent confirmed in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a business transaction between practitioner and client, examine whether the client received written advice to seek independent counsel, whether informed consent was obtained and confirmed in writing, and whether the transaction creates an adverse interest. Example: practitioner taking a 15% ownership interest in client company and not advising independent counsel violated §11.108(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of client-related information to client's disadvantage (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner is prohibited from using information relating to the representation of a client to the disadvantage of that client unless the client gives informed consent (note: § 11.108(b) does not require that such consent be confirmed in writing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether information developed during representation was later used in a way that disadvantaged the client (e.g., filing a patent application claiming sole inventorship based on work done while representing the client). Look for explicit client consent and whether consent met any required formality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective limitation of malpractice liability (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(h)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may not make an agreement prospectively limiting the practitioner's liability to a client for malpractice unless the client is independently represented in making the agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize contractual language that purports to waive or limit future malpractice claims; if such language exists, confirm whether the client had independent representation at the time and whether the limitation complies with §11.108(h)(1). Example: added clause 'will not ever be held accountable nor sued for damages' breached the rule where client lacked independent counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inform and explain; definition of informed consent (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.104(a)(1), 11.104(b), 11.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must promptly inform clients of any decision or circumstance requiring the client's informed consent. 'Informed consent' means the client's agreement to a proposed course of conduct after the practitioner has communicated adequate information and explanation about material risks and reasonably available alternatives. Practitioners must explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should verify timely communication of conflicts, adequate explanation of material risks and alternatives, and documentation where required. Failure to inform or explain can itself be a violation (e.g., not explaining that joint inventorship or business transactions create conflicts requiring consent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner-client relationship formation and attendant duties
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner-client relationship exists when a practitioner agrees to provide and provides services (e.g., patent prosecution). Once formed, the practitioner owes fiduciary duties to the client, including competence, communication, avoidance of conflicts, and protection of client interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than formal labels, look to conduct: filing applications, invoicing filing fees, providing services, and client reliance indicate a practitioner-client relationship. Once found, actions like accepting payment or filing applications implicate practitioner duties even if the practitioner later disputes the relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using practitioner's position to disadvantage or 'hold client hostage'
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not use their role, control of prosecution, or client-related information to coerce or disadvantage clients (e.g., by refusing to sign powers of attorney or to allow successor counsel to take over, causing abandonment of applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess conduct that impedes client's representation (refusing to transfer prosecution, charging ransom to assign applications) as potential violations of conflict/use-of-information rules and as harmful to client interests; such conduct can aggravate sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions determination factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b); ABA Standards guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing sanctions the Tribunal must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client/the public/the legal system/the profession; (2) the practitioner's mental state (intentional/knowing/negligent); (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors. The Tribunal often looks to the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions for guidance on severity and aggravating/mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the four regulatory factors and use ABA Standards to identify aggravating factors (e.g., dishonest or selfish motive; pattern of misconduct; refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing; substantial experience) and mitigating factors (e.g., no prior discipline). Examples from case: dishonest/selfish motive, pattern of misconduct, refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing, and substantial experience/no prior discipline were weighed to justify an 18‑month suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (examples drawn from ABA Standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors can include dishonest or selfish motive, pattern of misconduct, multiple offenses, refusal to acknowledge wrongful conduct, and substantial experience in the practice; mitigating factors can include lack of prior disciplinary history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List and weigh applicable factors when determining discipline. The record should support findings of motive, pattern, injury, and acceptance (or refusal) of responsibility. Use ABA Standards sections (e.g., §§9.22, 9.32) for analogues in sanctioning decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioners' duties while suspended and path to reinstatement (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.60(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: When suspended, practitioners are subject to duties set forth in §11.58; reinstatement requires petitioning the OED Director and complying with §11.60(c) procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions orders should direct respondents to the applicable suspension duties and the process for seeking reinstatement. Evaluators should note that suspension remains in effect until reinstatement is granted under the cited regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rule adherence in evaluating conduct (37 C.F.R. part 11; APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary evaluations and hearings must follow the procedural rules in 37 C.F.R. part 11 and the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 556), including provisions on impartial adjudicators, discovery/admission of evidence, summary judgment where appropriate, and post-hearing briefing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure procedural safeguards (notice, opportunity to be heard, impartial judge) are observed. Use summary judgment only where material facts are undisputed; otherwise, reserve disputed factual issues for hearing. Example: partial summary judgment was used for certain conflict findings here because facts were undisputed.
